title: Crosscheck Principle in Pediatric Audiology Today: A 40-Year Perspective
abstract: The crosscheck principle is just as important in pediatric audiology as it was when first described 40 years ago. That is, no auditory test result should be accepted and used in the diagnosis of hearing loss until it is confirmed or crosschecked by one or more independent measures. Exclusive reliance on only one or two tests, even objective auditory measures, may result in a auditory diagnosis that is not clear or perhaps incorrect. On the other hand, close and careful analysis of findings for a test battery consisting of objective procedures and behavioral tests whenever feasible usually leads to prompt and accurate diagnosis of auditory dysfunction. This paper provides a concise review of the crosscheck principle from its introduction to its clinical application today. The review concludes with a description of a modern test battery for pediatric hearing assessment that supplements traditional behavioral tests with a variety of independent objective procedures including aural immittance measures, otoacoustic emissions, and auditory evoked responses.

title: ASHA Recognizes Changemakers in Forensic Audiology
abstract: The future of audiology is built on the profession’s doctoral-level education steeped in science and ethics. Our specific knowledge is amassed upon incontrovertible research, scientific principles, best practices, and quantifiable outcomes that improve the quality of life for those we serve. Audiologists evaluate and manage a variety of audiovestibular complaints for patients across a broad age spectrum and with conditions that sometimes have legal liability. The etiology for hearing loss, tinnitus, hyperacusis, or a central auditory processing disorder may be a disease secondary to a physical injury. It is not uncommon for head and neck injuries, acoustic or blast trauma, and acute or continuous noise exposure to result in audiovestibular damage. Fortunately, many injuries recover within hours to days. However, the sequelae are long term and life altering for some. In some accident or negligence cases, hearing loss with an inability to detect acoustic warning signals can result in death. Not all hearing-related cases result from direct injury. The primary issues with hearing-related legal cases may be Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) entitlements, work readiness, community noise, malpractice, or education disputes. Other categories of audiology legal cases involve product liability, such as mass earplug litigation, patent infringement, or intellectual property disputes and other concerns. Sometimes, the injured party is not an individual but a company. All of these injuries, circumstances, or liability cases are within the purview of an audiologist.From left: James W. Hall, III, PhD; Robert M. Traynor, EdD, MBA; Thomas Powers, PhD; and Dennis A. Colucci, MA, AuD, ABAC, FAAA. Hearing Matters, ASHA, forensic audiology, expert witnessForensic audiology expert witnesses have existed for decades, but few clinicians understood how to or desired to interact with the legal system. For the most part, audiologists have lacked knowledge about expert witnesses and the role they play in the legal system. Professional witnesses are needed from every occupation, including audiology. Our advanced degrees, knowledge, skills, and abilities are sufficient credentials to assure the efficacy of audiologists as expert witnesses to the legal system. Our role as expert witnesses is codified by reimbursement rates paid to audiologists that support competency worthy of expert status equal to any other profession. Working as doctoral-level practitioners, applying the principles of research, evidenced-based diagnostic assessments, and up-to-date innovation in management have widened the scope of audiology to encompass the legal arena. Both AAA and ASHA include medical-legal and forensic practice within the profession’s scope of practice. ASHA 2023 The 2023 American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA) Convention included a Forensic Audiology session with presentations by Drs. Robert Traynor; James Hall, III; Tom Powers; and myself (Dennis Colucci). The session was one of only 117 ASHA 2023 Convention Changemaker Sessions selected out of a total of 3,400 submissions. Each Topic Committee could only recommend three top-rated sessions for this designation. The session consisted of a review of how and where forensic audiologists fit in the legal system, with specific insight into legal proceedings and how audiology principles and applications are used in various medical-legal cases. The presentation was well received. Participants walked away with pearls of wisdom on what the court needs and what it expects of expert witnesses, how our profession is positioned in the legal arena, the diagnostic knowledge and skills we can offer, the legal ramifications of technological innovation, and how audiologists develop a nexus and opine in court. To incorporate the essence of the ASHA Changemaker Session in this article, I asked the experts to write a brief answer to special questions related to principal areas audiologists need to understand to be effective expert witnesses. Dr. Christopher Spankovich has been asked to join this discussion because of his unique background in research as a practicing audiologist and NIH-funded scientist. Dr. Spankovich served as a general expert and case-specific expert for the largest mass tort case in U.S. history. Drs. Traynor, Hall, and Colucci also served as case-specific experts in this tort. The questions and answers revealed interesting perspectives concerning the process and principles important to forensic audiologist expert witnesses and clinicians alike. QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Process Principles—Robert M. Traynor, EdD, MBA Q: Dr. Traynor, it has been a longstanding view that audiologists are only trained to fit hearing aids and provide audiovestibular services. From your recent book “Forensic Audiology: A Guide for the Expert Witness,” can you tell us about the history of expert witness work and what position in the medical-legal realm audiology holds? A: Expert witnesses have been used in courts since Babylonian times. An English case, Folkes v. Chadd 1782-1783, began the vetting of expert witnesses when, on appeal, the Judge decided to use a civil engineer for information that decided a case that affected a major harbor in England. This began a 250-year precedent to use qualified experts in court. Expert witnesses were common in Europe but not in the United States until the 1920s. The case of Frye v. United States, 293F.1013/1014, 1922-23, involved a first-degree murder case that went to the U.S. Supreme Court. James Alphonso Frye lost his case in a lower court. Sentenced to life imprisonment, his attorneys wanted to use a lie detector to prove his innocence to the appeals court. The Judge would not allow the test or expert testimony. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Judge, disallowing the use of this evidence. Their ruling, known for 70 years (1923-1993) as the Frye Rule, was: “Expert testimony is ONLY allowed if founded upon Methods, Principles, and Procedures agreed upon as valid in the scientific community.” Well-researched, emerging science could not be used to support expert testimony unless it was considered valid by the whole of the scientific community within a discipline. The next generation in the vetting of expert witnesses was Daubert v. Merrell Pharmaceutical, Inc., 509 U.S., 1993; General Electric v. Joiner, 552 U.S. 136, 1997; and Kumho Tire Company v. Carmichael, 526 U.S., 1999. Known as the Daubert Trilogy, these cases set a new standard, updating and refining the expert vetting process, making judges the final authority for what expert testimony is allowed in court. Currently, judges consider the following criteria in vetting expert witnesses: The expert’s scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact understand the evidence or determine a fact in issue. The testimony is based on sufficient facts or data. The testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods. The expert has reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts of the case. Although there have been forensic audiologists for over 20 years, until recently, physicians offered most audiology written and oral testimony. For the most part, otolaryngology was the preferred choice of attorneys for expert testimony on hearing loss and balance cases. This was because audiology was a developing profession from the 1960s through the early 2000s, with a professional audiology education typically terminated with a master’s degree. Only 3% of audiologists earned a doctoral degree (PhD, EdD, or ScD) during this period. Although there were many master’s level audiologists clearly able to serve as expert witnesses, the lack of a doctorate prevented these professionals from being considered by attorneys as expert witnesses. The legal profession felt their clients were best served by physicians, specialized otolaryngologists, and/or the 3% of audiologists at the doctoral level for audiovestibular-related matters. The advent of the Doctor of Audiology (AuD) degree raised audiology to the doctoral level, forever changing the opinion of legal professionals seeking assistance. Since our training and experience are oriented differently, our patient experience is such that either an audiologist, an otolaryngologist, or both are appropriate for legal cases. Relative to legal cases and expert witnessing, audiologists should remember the phrase: “We are all doctors, some of us are physicians.” Diagnostic Principles—James W. Hall, III, PhD Q: Dr. Hall, can you tell our readers how you perceive the advances in testing now and in the future and how this knowledge, coupled with clinical skills, is used in forensic audiology? A: Evidence-based diagnostic principles should always undergird clinical audiology. The diagnostic principles that I’ve consistently applied in my career as an audiologist are appropriate also as guides for the clinical skills and knowledge required in forensic audiology. I’ve incorporated many new or updated clinical protocols and practices in audiology during the past 40+ years, but the diagnostic principles remain largely unchanged. An excellent example is the crosscheck principle, first eloquently described almost 50 years ago in the classic 1976 Jerger and Hayes paper.1 The crosscheck principle is remarkably simple and straightforward: the results of no single audiological test should be accepted until they are confirmed or “crosschecked” by the results of one or more independent measures of auditory function. Objective procedures invariably serve as “independent” measures within a diagnostic test battery for hearing assessment. Currently, the objective procedures most often applied in diagnostic audiological assessment of children and adults are aural immittance measures (tympanometry and acoustic reflexes), otoacoustic emissions (OAEs), and the auditory brainstem response (ABR). Objective procedures are especially important in forensic audiology because, by definition, they are not influenced by patient listener variables, including cooperation, motivation, and cognitive factors. Adherence to the crosscheck principle assures an audiologist that the results of diagnostic tests are valid and that the analysis of the test results will yield indisputable conclusions. Based on my experience in clinical and forensic audiology, I encourage all audiologists to regularly verify the outcome of behavioral hearing tests with findings for at least two different objective auditory procedures. Q: Would you please take a moment to provide us with a case-specific example to illustrate how the crosscheck principle is applied in forensic audiology? A: Certainly. As an audiology expert witness, I must address two issues that are almost always posed by triers of fact. Does the plaintiff have a hearing loss or related impairment (e.g., tinnitus, auditory process deficit, vestibular disorder)? And, if there is evidence of a hearing loss or related impairment answer, did it occur because of the defendant’s actions or omissions? To answer the first question, I am asked to conduct an independent audiological assessment to document the plaintiff’s hearing status. Alternatively, I may be asked to review findings for a hearing assessment conducted by another audiologist. Either way, I have an opportunity to determine which procedures are included in the test battery. My example, which I’ve encountered quite often, involves a plaintiff who claims to have a hearing loss resulting from some type of incident, either work-related or in the course of their usual activities. For this case, let’s assume the incident was work-related, and the defendant is the plaintiff’s employer, whereas I’m an expert witness for the defense (attorneys representing the defendant). My preferred test battery is weighted heavily toward objective auditory measures that will yield findings not influenced by the listener variables already noted. The test battery always includes procedures that assess the middle ear and cochlear function and permit objective estimation of auditory thresholds. Frequency specific ABR measurement is one objective option for estimation of auditory threshold. The auditory steady-state response (ASSR) is also an acceptable option. If there is a possibility that the incident could have caused a traumatic brain injury, I will invariably supplement the test battery with one or more objective measures of central auditory function, such as auditory middle latency or auditory late cortical evoked responses. In my opinion, there are no test time or financial constraints in designing a test battery for a forensic audiological assessment. The single all-important goal is to generate unequivocal factual evidence of peripheral and central auditory status. Innovation Principles—Thomas Powers, PhD Q: Dr. Powers, innovation and hearing science have brought remarkable changes to the hearing and balance impaired. How do you see your knowledge in electronics, instrumentation, measurement, and best practices in forensic audiology? What are the medical-legal ramifications for audiologists? A: I believe each of the areas mentioned above has contributed to my evolution into forensic audiology. During my PhD program, I was focused on electrophysiology measures at a time when the instrumentation for collection of this data was in its infancy. In those days, we had a rack of equipment that fits on my desktop today. Managing the interfaces for all the electronics was a major part of getting the research done. As I moved on to private practice and the hearing aid industry, I became immersed in hearing aid technology. Of course, the early devices were analog, but once the transition to digital procession occurred, the instrumentation became more complex and required much more understanding of product development and engineering principles. I attended long meetings with the engineering staff on signal processing and feature development that would form the basis of my interest in forensic audiology. I realized my expertise would fall best in the Intellectual Property (IP) area. Intellectual property is classified into four areas: trademarks, trade secrets, copyrights, and patents. The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) was established in 1790 to promote innovation. In exchange for submitting and publishing detailed information about an invention, the patent owner receives the right to exclude others from using that invention for the life of the patent. Since 1790, over 9 million patents have been awarded by the USPTO. During my time working in the hearing aid industry, I had extensive contact and involvement with the patent attorneys within our company. This provided valuable insights into the role patents play for a company and the work involved in defending them. It was clear that IP cases do not usually involve patient injuries that require diagnostic testing or expertise in the same manner needed in medical-legal cases. However, applying scientific principles and methods, conducting research, reviewing documents, opining, and providing written and oral testimony remain constants. Because the area of patent infringement seemed a match for the knowledge gained throughout my career, it has become valuable in establishing an expert witness component for my consulting company. In terms of best practices within patent infringement, an expert witness needs to have a clear understanding of the patent process and how the patent protects the invention. The expert witness must be able to communicate complicated technical issues within the patent to a jury. In addition, they must have the academic and professional background to be credible, much the same as expert witnesses in medical-legal cases. Forensic audiology is an exciting area of our field that can be very rewarding. It is not limited to physical injury but falls within the expertise of the audiology specialist. It requires extensive knowledge and experience and is attracting new participants. I encourage the readers to learn more and join us. Nexus and Opinion Principles—Dennis A. title: OBJECTIVE ASSESSMENT OF INFANT HEARING: ESSENTIAL FOR EARLY INTERVENTION
abstract: Substantial evidence supports the benefits of early intervention in infant hearing loss. Intervention can lead to the acquisition of effective communication skills and psychosocial development. Accurate diagnosis of infant hearing loss is not possible with conventional behavioral audiometry techniques. Objective auditory procedures are invaluable in the assessment of infant hearing because they do not rely on behavioral responses to sound and are unaffected by listener variables such as cognition, motivation, and language impairment. Objective hearing procedures include aural immittance measures (tympanometry and acoustic reflexes), otoacoustic emissions (OAEs), electrocochleography (ECochG), auditory brainstem response (ABR), and the auditory steady state response (ASSR). Exclusive reliance on only one or two objective auditory measures often results in equivocal outcomes. Careful analysis of findings from a comprehensive objective auditory test battery can almost always yield a precise description of auditory status; it can often lead to accurate diagnosis of auditory dysfunction within weeks of birth. The key to meaningful analysis of findings from a test battery is the recognition of patterns associated with major auditory disorders. This is not a novel concept; it is simply the modern day version of the 40-year-old cross-check principle.

title: Hearing help-seeking, hearing device uptake and hearing health outcomes in individuals with subclinical hearing loss: a systematic review
abstract: Objective This systematic review aims to examine the current literature on help-seeking, hearing device uptake, and hearing health outcomes in individuals with subclinical hearing loss.Design Systematic review.Study Sample Searches of three databases (CINAHL, MEDLINE (PubMed), and Scopus) yielded nine studies meeting the inclusion criteria. The quality of the included studies was determined using the National Institute of Health quality assessment tool. The studies’ level of evidence was determined according to the Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine.Results All included studies involved adult participants. Three studies examined help-seeking. Self-reported difficulty, poor speech-in-noise performance, and emotional responses to the hearing difficulty were identified as factors influencing help-seeking. Six studies examined the use of hearing devices as an intervention, including hearing aids (n = 4), hearables (n = 1), and FM systems (n = 1). Using hearing devices improved self-perceived hearing difficulty, speech-in-noise understanding, and motivation to address hearing difficulties. No studies focused on hearing device uptake. The quality assessment indicated limited methodological rigour across the studies, with varying levels of evidence.Conclusions Current evidence supports the use of hearing devices as an intervention for individuals with subclinical hearing loss. However, more research is essential, particularly focusing on help-seeking, diagnosis, treatment, and long-term outcomes using well-controlled study designs.

title: “The barriers are plentiful.” Speech-language pathologists’ perspectives of enablers and barriers to hearing assessment for children in metropolitan, regional, and rural Australia: A mixed methods study
abstract: PURPOSE: Access to hearing assessment is important for children, as poor auditory information can lead to poor speech and oral language development. This study aims to identify enablers and barriers to accessing hearing assessments for Australian children from the perspective of speech-language pathologists (SLPs), comparing access in metropolitan, regional, and rural areas. METHOD: This is a sequential, explanatory mixed-methods study. Forty-nine participants completed the quantitative survey and 14 participated in semi-structured interviews. The study was undertaken online and included participants from metropolitan, regional, and rural parts of Australian states and territories. RESULT: Similar accessibility issues were experienced across geographic locations and access to hearing assessment was related to the complexity of individual contexts. Speech-language pathologists felt that awareness and knowledge of hearing loss was low in parents and health professionals. Participants discussed barriers such as long wait times, complex criteria, and inefficient services that lead to compromised outcomes for clients. CONCLUSION: Barriers to hearing assessment are extensive and multifaceted. Future research might examine the accessibility of the health system in light of the barriers discussed in this research, and whether policies and procedures could be adapted to allow more easily accessible services.

title: How Do Audiologists Respond to Emotional and Psychological Concerns Raised in the Audiology Setting? Three Case Vignettes
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Emotional and psychological well-being are essential to overall health, but there is little research showing how to approach emotional and psychological concerns in the audiological setting. This study investigated audiologists' self-reported clinical behaviors in response to emotional and psychological concerns and/or symptoms raised by audiology clients. DESIGN: A sample of 83 Australia-based audiologists completed a survey including vignettes presenting older adults with hearing loss and experiencing symptoms consistent with either depression or grief. Content analysis was used to explore: (1) audiologists' self-reported usual response when clients present with emotional and psychological concerns and/or symptoms in the audiological setting; (2) audiologists' ability to identify and describe psychological symptoms; and (3) audiologists' self-reported clinical behaviors relating to client referral for psychological support. RESULTS: When asked to describe their usual clinical course of action in response to the vignettes, over one half the audiologists described actions that address the clients concerns related to psychological well-being. Where audiologists described how they would provide psychological support, they described modifications to the audiological rehabilitation program including involving significant others in the rehabilitation process, recommending additional support outside of the audiology setting (such as General Practitioner or psychologists), and providing emotional support and counseling. When prompted, the majority of participants recognized the two cases with depression as having a mental health condition; however, 48% of participants indicated the control case as also having a mental health condition. When asked directly, the majority of audiologists indicated that they would refer the three vignettes for specialist support; however, less than one third described referral to a General Practitioner and less than 5% described referral to a mental health professional as their normal course of action in the open response item. Twenty-five different professions/people were reported as potential sources for referral. CONCLUSION: These findings support the need for further training and/or resources for audiologists to enable them to appropriately detect, describe and refer for emotional and psychological concerns and/or symptoms raised by clients' in the audiology setting.

title: Online reviews of hearing aid acquisition and use : A qualitative thematic analysis
abstract: Online reviews have become increasingly common for consumers to share their experiences about products and to assist potential consumers with decision making. The current study was aimed to understand the hearing aid user experience from online consumer reviews using qualitative analysis.The study used a qualitative thematic analysis to analyze open text responses from consumers leaving hearing aid reviews on the http://www.HearingTracker.com website. One thousand three hundred seventy-eight online consumer hearing aid reviews (open-text responses) were extracted and analyzed.Three domains emerged within the data set, containing 11 themes and 136 subthemes. Domain one (Clinical Processes) contained two themes: Hearing Assessment and Hearing Aid Acquisition. Domain two (The Device) contained five themes: Function, Performance, Physical, Device Management, and Maintenance. Domain three (The Person) contained four themes: Satisfaction, Quality of Life, Personal Adjustment, and Knowledge. The themes gave an understanding that there were a contribution of factors that formed part of a consumers hearing aid user experience.Hearing aid users described a range of positive, negative, and neutral descriptions online about their hearing aid user experience and gave advice to fellow hearing aid users helping clinicians improve their hearing aid fitting skills in practice. These findings have implications to future product development as well as service delivery model in terms of developing strategies for fostering patient-centered audiological practice.

title: Deaf Sign Language users and Audiology Services: A scoping review on cultural competence
abstract: Review question / Objective: This study aims to identify culturally competent practice in audiology services from service provider and adult Deaf sign language users’ perspectives. Therefore, the questions are as follows: (1) Are audiology services providing culturally competent practice to adult patients who are Deaf sign language users? (2) What are adult Deaf sign language users’ experiences of audiology services from the perspective of cultural competence? Information sources: The following databases will be used: PubMed, Embase, CINHAL, PsychInF0, Web of Science SSCI and Project Muse. Grey literature (for example, guidelines, policies, and practice documents) will be searched. Also, key journals, reference lists and grey literature will be searched for additional references. There will be no publication date restriction to avoid excluding papers identified in non-indexed papers. The search date for each database and platform will be reported.

title: Audiologic Assessment of Preschool Children with Hearing Loss in a Secondary Health Care Setting
abstract: The study aimed to evaluate the audiologic profile of preschool children with hearing loss, i.e., to determine the type, degree, and configuration of hearing loss, amplitude of otoacoustic emissions, and word recognition performance. This retrospective study included 260 children examined in a secondary healthcare setting. For statistical data analysis, we used the Chi-square test with a level of significance p < 0.05. Conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss was present in 93.1%, 4.6%, and 2.3%, respectively. Mild hearing loss was present in 96.1%, moderate in 2.3%, and severe hearing loss in 1.6%. Type B tympanogram was the most common (p = 0.00001). The mean amplitude of otoacoustic emissions was -7.6 dB in sensorineural hearing loss and 12.3 dB in normal hearing. The maximum word recognition score was frequently obtained at presentation levels of 25-40 dB SL (p = 0.009). The majority of children had mild conductive hearing loss with normal word recognition ability.

title: Autism and hearing loss: Recommendations for improved diagnostic evaluations and interventions
venue: The Knowledge Bank (The Ohio State University)
abstract: The goal of this paper is to review the existing literature about hearing loss and autism and make recommendations based upon these findings to improve diagnostic techniques, intervention programs, and hearing aid outcomes. Autism continues to be on the rise worldwide as well in the United States. Audiologists are typically the first professionals who have contact with a child who is suspected of autism. This paper examines the audiologist’s role in making appropriate referrals if they suspect a child has a developmental difficulties. In addition, the paper will examine the audiologist’s role in the management of children with hearing loss and autism. Also, the paper will discuss the audiologist’s role on a diagnostic/therapeutic team for a child suspected of a developmental disorder. The characteristics of autism and how they impact the audiological evaluation will be discussed. Specific recommendations will address modifications that can help improve the behavioral audiological process. Intervention and hearing aid plans that address the unique needs of children with hearing loss and autism will be examined. Finally, the paper will present recommendations for future study in the area of autism and hearing loss.

title: Learning outcomes of speech audiometry virtual patient use for expert and novice audiology students
abstract: Rationale: Audiology student training in New Zealand faces many difficulties with a limited number of qualified instructors and suitable external placements. With a continued shortage of audiologists in New Zealand, new methods of training need to be introduced and implemented. One solution is through the use of realistic, computer-based virtual patient simulators (VPS). HIT Lab New Zealand in conjunction with the University of Canterbury has designed a VPS for New Zealand audiology students. A speech audiometry component is to be developed based on best practice recommendations, and needs to be validated. Method: Two studies, one with 18 Master of Audiology (“expert”) and another with 18 (“novice”) undergraduate students, were evenly divided into simulator and non-simulator user groups. Simulator users had to complete 5 virtual patient cases in addition to the non-simulator users’ requirement to refer to provided lecture notes and speech audiometry protocols. Novice students were assessed on declarative, procedural and retained knowledge of speech audiometry; expert students were additionally assessed on training transfer. The intervention period was set at two weeks, and the retention assessment at four weeks post-intervention. Results: Expert students who used the simulator significantly improved their training transfer skills. No significant differences were found between and within groups for declarative knowledge and procedural knowledge. Training transfer and procedural knowledge were retained for both groups, but only non-simulator users retained declarative knowledge. Novice students who used the simulator significantly increased their declarative knowledge. Both groups’ procedural knowledge significantly regressed post-intervention. Declarative and procedural knowledge were retained for both groups. Implications: Simulator use appears to accelerate learning outcomes otherwise achievable through traditional learning methods, and does depend on the users’ existing knowledge base. Regular use may be necessary to retain desired learning outcomes. Improvements (e.g., more detailed feedback systems) are to be incorporated into the simulator, and sole reliance on the simulator for learning is not recommended. Future research into more holistic aspects of virtual patient use within the field of audiology and allied health care is warranted.

title: Towards the Development of the New Zealand Hearing in Noise Test (NZHINT)
abstract: The ability to understand speech in noise has a profound impact on everyday communication, but cannot be predicted on the basis of puretone thresholds and/or performance on tests of speech in quiet. The aim of this thesis was to develop an adaptive speech in noise test based on the Hearing in Noise Test (HINT) that would be reliable and valid for speakers of New Zealand English (NZE). The methodology used followed the standard procedures for developing the HINT in a new language. Five hundred sentences of 5-7 syllables were collected from New Zealand children’s books and recorded by a native NZE speaker. Nine normal-hearing native NZE speakers aged 18-50 listened to three sets of 50 sentences at -2, -4 and -7 dB signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) in order to establish a performance-intensity (PI) function for these sentences. Three groups of 10 participants were scored on their performance on the sentences in 65 dBA speech-weighted noise at varying SNR. After each round of testing with a new group of participants, the SNR of each sentence was adjusted in order to get closer to 70% intelligibility for all sentences. Sentences that were too easy or difficult or did not respond to adjustments were discarded. Once the remaining 240 sentences were of approximately equal intelligibility, 24 phonemically matched lists of 10 sentences were formed and tested on 12 participants using the adaptive HINT software. The overall mean threshold was calculated as -6 dB, s.d=1.1 dB. The lists were combined to form 12 lists of 20 sentences which would become the NZHINT. Time delays meant that the collection of normative data could not be completed.
